analysis.one_liner: Turns serious willful workplace safety violations into crimes with up to 20-year prison terms.
analysis.headline: The bill to criminally punish employers for willfully injuring or endangering workers died in a House subcommittee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have raised the stakes for employers who break federal workplace safety rules. Willful violations that seriously injure a worker could bring up to 7 years in prison (up to 14 for repeat offenders), and violations that recklessly endanger life could bring up to 5 years. It would also make corporate directors and officers personally liable — with prison time and fines they could not pay out of company money — if they willfully authorized or tolerated a safety violation, and it clarified that states could prosecute these cases under their own laws.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers in hazardous industries. Current OSHA law treats a willful safety violation that kills a worker as a misdemeanor punishable by at most six months in jail; this bill would have made serious injury or reckless endangerment a felony with real prison exposure, and made the executives behind the decision personally answerable rather than leaving the company's insurance or treasury to absorb the fine.

how_it_helps.text: A willful OSHA violation causing serious bodily injury to an employee would become a crime punishable by up to 7 years in prison, or up to 14 years for repeat offenders; a willful violation that recklessly endangers life would carry up to 5 years, or 10 for repeat offenders. [S3]

Prison terms for existing OSHA crimes would rise sharply: from six months to 10 years for a willful violation causing an employee's death, from one year to 20 years for a second such conviction, and from six months to 2 years for giving advance notice of an inspection, with fines set under the general federal criminal fine statute instead of fixed small dollar caps. [S3]

Directors, officers, or agents who willfully authorize, order, or acquiesce in a safety violation would face the same fines and prison terms as the employer, and any fine imposed on them personally could not be paid out of company assets — putting the consequence on the decision-maker rather than the corporate treasury. [S3]
The bill states that nothing in OSHA prevents state and local law enforcement from prosecuting employers under state criminal laws, preserving an additional path to accountability. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Employers and their executives who willfully violate safety rules: they would face felony-level fines, multi-year prison terms, and personal liability for officers and directors. Employers generally would bear the cost of stricter compliance and the risk of prosecution for violations that injure workers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers and executives who violate safety rules

drawbacks.text: The bill sets the bar for criminal liability at 'recklessly endangers' and defines serious bodily injury broadly, including extreme physical pain or protracted impairment, so employers and their lawyers would argue that ordinary workplace accidents could be prosecuted as crimes, raising liability risk beyond the clear-cut cases of willful endangerment. [S3]

The new exposure would fall on individual officers and directors personally, with fines they cannot pay from corporate funds — a cost that good-faith critics would call disproportionate for mid-level managers caught in a violation someone above them ordered. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the benefit is real: under the law as it stood, a willful safety violation that killed an employee carried a maximum of six months in jail, a penalty widely regarded as too small to change corporate behavior. The main cost is that the criminal thresholds in the bill — especially 'reckless endangerment' and the broad injury definition — could sweep in cases short of true willfulness, and that risk would fall partly on individual managers. On balance the bill addressed a gap where worker deaths carried less criminal exposure than many nonviolent offenses, though its breadth would have invited litigation over where liability lines fall.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Education and Labor Committee, which passed it down to its Health and Safety Subcommittee in March 1991, where it stayed until the Congress ended — no hearing or vote is recorded.

narrative.text: Rep. Tom Lantos introduced the OSHA Criminal Penalty Reform Act on February 28, 1991, joined by 19 cosponsors. [S1]
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor the day it was introduced. [S5]

On March 21, 1991, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health and Safety, and the record shows no further action — no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — before the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who violate workplace safety rules, and the directors and officers who would have faced personal fines and prison time under the bill, are better off because it never advanced: the criminal penalties in OSHA law stayed at their pre-1991 levels, with a willful violation that kills a worker still carrying a maximum of six months in jail.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers and executives facing no new liability

for.name: Rep. Tom Lantos
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to raise OSHA criminal penalties and hold corporate officers personally liable for willful safety violations.

for.name: 19 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support; the group included 17 Democrats, 1 Independent, and 1 Republican, among them Reps. Barney Frank and Nancy Pelosi. [S4]

against.name: House Education and Labor Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill beyond receiving the referral; never scheduled a markup or committee vote. [S5]

against.name: Subcommittee on Health and Safety
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on March 21, 1991, and the record shows no hearings, markup, or vote; the bill sat there until the Congress ended. [S5]

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Democratic — 17 of the 19 cosponsors were Democrats — with one Independent and one Republican; no recorded floor or committee vote ever showed where the full chamber stood.

industries.industry: Employers in OSHA-covered industries (manufacturing, construction, and other hazardous workplaces)
industries.note: The bill would have exposed them to felony-level fines and multi-year prison terms for willful violations that injure or recklessly endanger workers, and to state prosecutions on top of federal ones. Because the bill died, their criminal exposure stayed at the old misdemeanor-level caps.

The bill would have made them personally liable — with prison time and fines that could not be paid from corporate assets — when they willfully authorized or tolerated a safety violation. The bill's death left this personal-liability exposure out of federal law.
